summary: Alcantarí International Airport (SRE) serves Sucre, the constitutional capital of Bolivia and a UNESCO World Heritage city known for its well-preserved colonial architecture. Opened in 2016, the airport replaced the older Juana Azurduy de Padilla Airport, which was situated within city limits and had challenging approach procedures due to surrounding hills. Located approximately 30 km southwest of Sucre at a high elevation of around 3,000 meters, it provides safer modern operations for the region.
faqs:
Q: What is the distance from Alcantarí Airport to Sucre city center?
A: The airport is located approximately 30 km (about 19 miles) southwest of Sucre's historic center, with typical journey times of 45-60 minutes by road.

Q: Which airlines operate at Alcantarí International Airport?
A: Boliviana de Aviación (BoA) and Amaszonas are the main carriers operating domestic flights connecting Sucre with La Paz, Santa Cruz, and Cochabamba.

Q: Why was the new airport built outside Sucre?
A: The previous airport had limited runway length and difficult approach conditions due to the mountainous terrain surrounding Sucre. The new location at Alcantarí allows larger aircraft operations and safer landings.

Q: Is the airport affected by altitude?
A: Yes, at roughly 3,000 meters above sea level, passengers may experience mild altitude effects, and aircraft performance is factored into flight operations from this high-elevation airfield.
transport_tips: Taxis and private transfers are the most common ways to reach Sucre from the airport; pre-booking through your hotel is recommended for a fixed rate and reliable service. Shared minibuses occasionally operate but are infrequent and less reliable for catching specific flights. The road journey involves winding mountain roads, so allow extra time, especially during rainy season when visibility can be reduced.
local_tip: Request a window seat on the left side during arrival for spectacular views of Sucre's white colonial buildings nestled in the Andean valley—it's one of the most photogenic approaches in South America, especially on clear mornings.
